new_prompt:
Design a 3:4 vertical poster split into a 3x3 grid that can be sliced into nine separate carousel images.

Inputs
- Theme: [e.g. better sleep tips]
- Audience: [e.g. busy young professionals]
- Brand colours: [default: cream white, beige, light caramel, dark brown text]

Layout
- Tile 1: cover with a bold title (max 6 words) and a one-line hook.
- Tiles 2-9: one tip each, with a heading (max 5 words), one or two plain sentences, and a small flat illustration of [an object that matches the tip].
- Centre each tile's content and keep 8% margins and clear gutters, so every tile reads on its own once sliced.

Rules: one idea per tile, no tiny text, no claims you can't back up, consistent illustration style across all nine.

Write an email asking a reference about a job candidate.

Inputs
- Reference: [name, relationship to candidate]
- Candidate: [name]
- Role I'm hiring for: [title, organisation]
- What the role needs most: [2-3 items, e.g. supervising students, heavy admin, parent communication]
- My deadline: [date]

Output
- Subject line.
- Body under 200 words: thank them, explain the role in one sentence, then a numbered list of 4-5 questions covering strengths, areas for growth, how the candidate would handle [the key needs], and anything else they'd like to share.
- Offer a 15-minute phone call as an alternative, with [my availability].
- Sign-off with [my name, title, phone].

Tone: professional and warm. Don't ask for confidential HR records.

new_title: 1980s Magazine Ad for a Modern Product
new_prompt:
Create a fictional full-page 1980s magazine advertisement for a modern product.

Inputs
- Product: [name and what it does, e.g. an AI writing assistant]
- Headline: "[headline]"
- Tagline: "[tagline]"
- 3 features: [features]

Composition (portrait, 8.5x11 proportions)
- Top: chrome 3D headline with a starburst highlight; tagline beneath in yellow italic script.
- Centre: a beige 1980s home computer on a wood-grain desk, a cheerful family gathered around the glowing screen showing the product.
- Bottom: small-print feature list with bullet icons, a fake price and phone number box, and a placeholder logo.

Style: offset-print texture, slight colour fringing, warm faded palette, period-accurate typography. No real brand logos.

new_title: Anagram Puzzle List With Answer Check
new_prompt:
Create 10 anagram puzzles whose answers all start with the letter [letter].

Rules
- Answers are common English words of [5-8] letters (no proper nouns).
- Each anagram must use exactly the same letters as its answer, rearranged, and must not be the answer itself.
- Mix difficulty: 4 easy, 4 medium, 2 hard.

Output: a numbered list in this exact format:
(#): ANAGRAM • ANSWER • difficulty

Before finalising, check every pair letter by letter and replace any pair that doesn't match. Finish with one line confirming the check was done.

new_title: Turn Facts Into a Dramatic Monologue
new_prompt:
Recast the passage below as a stage monologue without losing a single fact.

Inputs
- Passage: [paste]
- Speaker: [who is talking, e.g. a museum curator on the night the exhibit closes]
- Audience on stage: [who they address]
- Length: [e.g. 250-350 words, about 2 minutes spoken]

Requirements
- Every fact in the passage appears, accurately; add emotion, rhythm and imagery, never new facts or dates.
- Open with a line that grabs attention, build to a turning point, and end on a strong closing line.
- Include 2-3 bracketed stage directions, e.g. [pauses].

After the monologue, list each fact from the passage and the line where it appears, so I can check nothing was dropped.

new_title: Bullet Summary of a Big Idea
new_prompt:
Explain [philosophy, movement or theory, e.g. Stoicism] to a curious beginner.

Output
1. One-sentence definition.
2. Up to 10 bullets, one idea each, in plain words (no jargon unless you define it), ordered: core belief → key concepts → famous figures or texts → common misunderstandings → how people practise it today.
3. 'Try this' box: one small exercise a reader could do this week.
4. Two reputable starting points for further reading, with author and title. Don't invent sources; if unsure, say so.

Keep the whole answer under [250] words and stay neutral; present it, don't advocate for it.

new_title: Summarize a News Article for a Newcomer
new_prompt:
Summarise the article below for someone who hasn't followed the story.

Inputs
- Article: [paste]
- Length: [e.g. 5 sentences]
- Reader: [e.g. a busy manager, a student]

Output
- Headline (max 10 words).
- Summary: lead with the main news, include the key numbers and who is involved, give one sentence of background, and end with why it matters to [reader].
- 'What we don't know yet': 1-2 bullets, if the article leaves open questions.

Rules: use only facts from the article, keep names and figures exact, and don't add opinion.

Design a set of three promotional banners for a strawberry campaign in a bright, cheerful anime illustration style.

Inputs
- Brand / product: [name]
- Mascot: [adult character description]
- Colour theme: [e.g. strawberry red, cream and mint]
- Offer: [e.g. 20% off this weekend]

Deliverables
1. Wide web banner (3:1): mascot left, strawberries cascading right, headline and CTA button.
2. Square social post (1:1): mascot holding a basket of strawberries, headline on top, offer badge.
3. Vertical story (9:16): mascot full-body, strawberry pattern background, CTA at the bottom.

Keep the mascot, typography and palette identical across all three; headline max 6 words; CTA: "[CTA text]".

new_title: Jewelry as a Miniature City Ad
new_prompt:
Create a luxury jewellery advertisement where the piece becomes a monument in a tiny city.

Inputs
- Piece: [e.g. a diamond and ruby necklace]
- Brand name: [name]
- Line of copy: "[short line]"

Scene
- The jewellery stands huge at the centre like a landmark, lit like a monument at night.
- A miniature futuristic city grows around and through it: towers, bridges, roads, tiny people looking up.
- Dark navy background, warm spotlights on the stones, sharp macro detail on facets and metal.

Layout: portrait 4:5, brand name in fine serif capitals at the bottom, the copy line above it, generous empty space. No real brand logos.

Write a deadpan persuasive email that argues an absurd case so convincingly that it's funny.

Inputs
- Recipient: [e.g. my school principal]
- Playful claim: [e.g. Pig Latin should count as my foreign-language credit]
- What I'm asking for: [e.g. a proficiency exam]
- One real detail about me: [detail]

Structure (under 250 words)
1. Respectful opening and the request in one sentence.
2. Three numbered arguments, each 'serious' and well-reasoned (history, precedent, practical benefit).
3. Pre-empt the obvious objection.
4. Polite close with a specific next step.

Tone: formal and earnest throughout; the humour comes from the logic, never from winking at the reader. Keep it kind.

Act as a senior product manager and write a product requirements document.

Inputs
- Feature or product: [name, one-line description]
- Users: [who has the problem]
- Constraints: [deadline, platforms, budget, tech limits]
- Known data: [metrics, research, support tickets]

First, ask me up to five questions if key details are missing; then write the PRD.

PRD sections (max two pages)
1. Problem & who has it (evidence from my inputs only)
2. Goals and success metrics (how we'll measure each)
3. User stories ("As a…, I want…, so that…")
4. Functional requirements (numbered, testable)
5. Out of scope
6. Risks & mitigations
7. Open questions

Write so an engineer and a designer can both start work from it. Mark assumptions as ASSUMPTION.

new_title: Beginner How-To Article on a Home Repair
new_prompt:
Write a beginner-friendly how-to article on a home repair.

Inputs
- Repair: [e.g. patching holes in drywall]
- Length: [e.g. under 700 words]
- Region / currency for costs: [e.g. India, INR]

Structure
1. Intro: what this fixes and how long it takes.
2. Tools & materials: bulleted list, with an approximate cost range for each marked 'approx.'.
3. Step-by-step for small jobs, then a separate set for large jobs, numbered.
4. Safety notes.
5. Common mistakes (3 bullets).
6. When to call a professional.

Rules: plain language, one action per step, and don't state exact prices as facts; give ranges and say they vary.

Write a humorous job posting that still reads like a real advert.

Inputs
- Unusual role: [e.g. professional recliner tester at a furniture company]
- Company: [name, one quirky detail]
- Location / pay: [details or 'competitive']

Format (under 250 words)
- Job title (with a pun if it fits)
- About us (2 sentences)
- What you'll do (4 bullets)
- What you'll need (4 bullets, mixing real skills with absurd ones)
- Perks (3 bullets)
- How to apply (1 line)

Tone: dry, playful, workplace-appropriate; no jokes about age, gender, disability or appearance.

Create profiles for five characters whose superpowers are strange, and who use them in surprising, everyday ways.

Inputs
- Setting: [e.g. a small coastal town, modern day]
- Tone: [e.g. cosy and funny / bittersweet]
- Audience: [e.g. middle-grade readers]

For each character (under 80 words each, under 400 total)
- Name and one-line identity
- Power (specific and limited, e.g. 'can hear what houseplants need')
- How they actually use it (a concrete example)
- One flaw or cost of the power

Make the five powers distinct from each other and avoid famous existing heroes.

new_title: Fun Fan Blog Post With Headings
new_prompt:
Write a short, chatty blog post from the point of view of a long-time fan.

Inputs
- Topic: [e.g. a 90s pop group]
- Fan's angle: [e.g. why their debut still holds up]
- Length: [e.g. 600-800 words]

Structure (mark headings exactly as shown)
- Title
- Intro paragraph
- [H2] section one, with two [H3] subsections
- [H2] section two, with one [H3] subsection
- Closing paragraph with a question for readers

Rules: fun, personal tone; facts must be accurate (if unsure about a date or chart position, leave it out or mark it [VERIFY]); no copied lyrics.

Create a vertical (4:5) food advertisement where a crisps packet erupts into a place's flavours and landmarks.

Inputs
- Place: [city or country]
- Flavour name on the packet: [e.g. 'Mumbai Street Masala']
- 3-4 signature foods or spices: [list]
- 2-3 landmarks: [list]

Composition
- Bottom centre: a realistic, crinkled crisps packet with the flavour name and place on the label (no real brands).
- Rising from it: a spiral of sauces, spices, steam and the signature dishes, transforming into the landmarks at the top.
- Bright commercial lighting, saturated but appetising colour, crisp detail on the crisps themselves.

Add a short headline at the top: "[headline]".

Design a 16:9 reaction-video thumbnail that reads instantly at phone size.

Inputs
- Character: an adult anime character with [hair colour] hair, cat ears and purple eyes
- Expression: [e.g. shocked, sweating]
- Headline: "[max 4 words]"
- What she's reacting to: [object or screenshot]

Layout
- Character on the right third, large, cropped at the chest, strong outline.
- Left: the headline in heavy rounded type with a thick stroke.
- A red arrow pointing from the character to [the thing she's reacting to].
- Background: neon pink and black with paint splatters.

Rules: high contrast, max 3 colours plus black, nothing important in the bottom-right corner (timestamp area).

new_title: Python: Download a CSV From a URL
new_prompt:
Write a production-ready Python function that downloads a CSV file from a URL and saves it locally.

Requirements
- Signature: `download_csv(url: str, dest_path: str, timeout: int = 30) -> str` returning the saved path.
- Use `requests` with streaming (`iter_content`, 1 MB chunks) so large files don't load into memory.
- Raise a clear exception with the status code on non-2xx responses; handle timeouts and connection errors.
- Write to a temporary file first, then rename, so a failed download never leaves a half file.
- Create parent folders if missing.

Output
1. The function with docstring and type hints.
2. A short usage example.
3. How to load the result into pandas (`pd.read_csv`), including an encoding fallback.
4. Two pytest tests using a mocked response.

Act as a customer-support QA reviewer and grade the replies below.

Inputs: [paste each customer message and agent reply as numbered pairs]
Company tone guide: [optional, e.g. friendly, no jargon]

For each pair, output a row in a table with these columns:
| # | Rating (Excellent / Good / Poor) | Solved the problem? (Y/N) | Owned any mistake? (Y/N) | Tone respectful? (Y/N) | Reason (max 2 sentences) | Improved reply (only if not Excellent, under 80 words) |

After the table: the three most common issues across all replies, and one coaching tip for each.

Judge only what is in the text; don't assume details the customer didn't give.

Write a birthday letter to a child from their favourite superhero.

Inputs
- Child: [name, age]
- Hero: [e.g. a caped detective hero]
- 2-3 true details about the child: [e.g. learned to ride a bike, loves dinosaurs, is kind to their sister]
- Message from the parent to weave in: [e.g. keep being brave at the new school]

Requirements
- 150-200 words, in the hero's voice and style.
- Mention every detail naturally; praise effort and kindness, not just achievements.
- Include one small 'secret mission' the child can do this week.
- End with a sign-off the hero would use.

Keep it age-appropriate, warm, and free of anything scary.

Turn a company's annual report into a memo for my team.

Inputs
- Report: [paste or attach]
- Company: [name]
- Our relationship to them: [e.g. we sell to them / compete with them]
- Our industry: [industry]

Memo (under 400 words)
1. Subject line.
2. How they did this year, in three sentences.
3. Numbers that matter: revenue, profit, margins and major changes, as bullets with the year-on-year change.
4. Trends these point to in [industry].
5. What this means for us: opportunities, risks, and one recommended action.

Rules: use only figures from the report and cite the page or section for each; mark interpretation as 'Our read:'; flag anything unclear rather than guessing.

new_title: Answer a Question From a Book Passage
new_prompt:
Answer a question using only a passage I provide.

Inputs
- Book and author: [details]
- Question: [question]
- Passage: [paste]

Output
1. Answer: one or two sentences.
2. Evidence: the exact quoted line(s) from the passage that support it.
3. Confidence: High / Medium / Low, with one sentence explaining why.

Rules: don't use outside knowledge of the book. If the passage doesn't contain the answer, say 'Not in the passage' and explain what would be needed.

Write a short in-store intercom announcement.

Inputs
- Store name: [name]
- Motto: "[motto]"
- Today's highlight (optional): [e.g. fresh bakery items at 5 pm]
- Tone: [e.g. friendly and upbeat]

Requirements
- Exactly four sentences, about 20 seconds when read aloud.
- Order: greeting with the store name, thank-you for shopping, the highlight (or a helpful tip if none), and the motto as the final words.
- Easy to say aloud: short words, no abbreviations or symbols.

Give two alternative versions: one standard and one for a holiday period.

new_title: Light Limerick on a Chosen Subject
new_prompt:
Write a playful limerick about [subject, e.g. a cat who believes it owns the neighbourhood].

Rules
- Five lines, AABBA rhyme.
- Lines 1, 2 and 5 have three stressed beats; lines 3 and 4 have two.
- Clean, family-friendly humour, with a twist in the last line.
- Use [one detail to include, e.g. the cat's name, Biscuit].

Output: the limerick, then a second alternative, then one line naming the twist in each. Read each aloud in your head and fix any line where the rhythm stumbles.

Write a short memoir from an unexpected point of view.

Inputs
- Narrator: [e.g. a goldfish on a family's kitchen counter]
- The people around it: [who they are]
- Tone: [e.g. wry and tender]
- Length: [under 400 words]

Requirements
- First person, past tense, in a voice that fits the narrator's limited view of the world.
- Show what it notices that humans miss, and what it thinks of the people.
- Build to one memorable event, with a small emotional shift at the end.
- Use concrete sensory detail; avoid explaining the joke.

Give it a title.

new_title: Turn a News Item Into Fiction
new_prompt:
Rewrite a news story as an excerpt from a novel, keeping the real facts intact.

Inputs
- News story: [paste]
- Genre: [e.g. near-future thriller]
- Point of view: [e.g. a junior reporter, first person]
- Length: [e.g. 400-600 words]

Requirements
- Keep every factual element (who, what, where, when, numbers) accurate; invent only scene, inner thoughts and dialogue.
- Open in the middle of action, build tension, and end on a hook.
- Don't put invented quotes in the mouths of real, named people; use fictional characters for dialogue.

After the excerpt, list the real facts used, so I can check them.

new_title: Rework a Poem Into a Rhyme Scheme
new_prompt:
Rewrite a poem so it follows a set rhyme scheme while keeping its meaning.

Inputs
- Poem: [paste]
- Target scheme: [e.g. ABAB CDCD]
- Metre (optional): [e.g. iambic tetrameter]

Output
1. The rewritten poem.
2. The rhyme letters marked at the end of each line.
3. A short note listing the lines where you changed the wording most, and why.

Rules: keep the original imagery and as much wording as possible; prefer true rhymes over slant rhymes; don't add new ideas.

new_title: 2x2 Grid of Ads for Four Industries
new_prompt:
Create a 2x2 grid of four advertisements that works as a design-portfolio sample.

Inputs
- Industries: [1 e.g. skincare], [2], [3], [4]
- Language for copy: [language]

For each ad (square tile)
- An invented brand name and simple logo mark (no real brands).
- A photo-style hero image suited to the industry.
- A headline (max 6 words) and one supporting line (max 12 words).

Consistency rules: same grid spacing and type system across all four, but each ad gets its own colour palette and mood so the range shows. Thin white gutters between tiles.

Design a high-energy drink advertisement, 4:5 portrait.

Inputs
- Drink name / flavour: [e.g. 'Volt Strawberry']
- Headline: "[max 5 words]"
- Model: an athletic adult in a light jacket, orange shorts and white trainers

Composition
- Background: bright orange gradient.
- Mid-ground: the model mid-jump, with strawberry juice and ice cubes splashing around her in an arc.
- Foreground: a cold can beaded with condensation, fresh strawberries on a glossy surface, sharp focus.
- Headline in bold italic sans-serif across the top; small product line at the bottom.

Style: crisp commercial photography, frozen motion, saturated reds and oranges. No real brand logos.

Create a single explainer slide that mixes cute, friendly flat clip-art illustrations with the packed, everything-on-one-page layout of an official government briefing slide.

Inputs
- Topic: [e.g. a folk tale, a new policy, a process]
- Key points to include: [5-8 points]
- Language: [language]

Layout (16:9)
- Title band across the top.
- 6-8 boxed sections connected by arrows, each with a heading, one short sentence and a small illustration.
- A summary box at the bottom right.

Rules: dense but readable (minimum text size equivalent to 14pt), consistent illustration style, and accurate content only from my key points.

Make a step-by-step recipe flowchart sized 3:4 for a social post.

Inputs
- Dish: [e.g. chilli stir-fried pork]
- Servings: [number]
- Ingredients with amounts: [list, or ask me to confirm yours]

Layout
- Top: dish name, total time and difficulty, then the ingredient list in two columns.
- Below: 5-8 steps as connected boxes, each with a realistic photo of that stage, a short label (max 8 words) and a key detail (heat level, time).
- Bottom: one tip for getting it right.

Rules: steps in the correct cooking order, safe cooking temperatures for meat, consistent photo lighting.

new_title: Summer Soda Ad Built for Clicks
new_prompt:
Design a 3:4 summer advertisement photo for a soft drink.

Inputs
- Drink name: "[name]", 500 ml bottle
- Flavour: [flavour]
- Offer line: [e.g. 'Buy 2, get 1 free']

Before generating, choose three attention techniques that suit drink ads (for example: one bold colour block, cold condensation and ice, a clearly readable offer) and state them in one line.

Then create the image: the bottle large and in focus, condensation and ice, summery props in [setting], the offer in a high-contrast badge, the drink name legible. No real brands. Finally, give one alternative headline.

Write a short absurd story that fully commits to a ridiculous premise.

Inputs
- Premise: [odd premise, e.g. a toilet that can see ghosts]
- Main character: [who]
- Length: 200-300 words

Requirements
- Treat the premise completely seriously; the humour comes from logic, not winks.
- Clear beginning (normal life plus the oddity), middle (escalation), and end (resolution).
- At least one specific, vivid detail per paragraph.
- Land on a surprising or funny final line.

Give it a title, and keep it suitable for a general audience.

Write a short fish-out-of-water story.

Inputs
- Character: [name and one trait]
- Their world, where they excel: [e.g. alpine skiing]
- Unfamiliar situation: [e.g. a night shift at a busy diner]
- Tone: [funny or warm]
- Length: under 300 words

Requirements
- Show their expertise in the opening lines, then drop them into the new situation.
- Three escalating mistakes, each caused by applying their old skills wrongly.
- A turning point where one old skill unexpectedly helps.
- An ending that shows what they learned.

Give it a title.

new_title: First-Month Plan for a New Hobby or Platform
new_prompt:
I'm starting [activity, e.g. streaming on Twitch]. Help me get through the first month.

About me: [experience level, hours per week, budget, goal]

Output
1. Setup checklist (essential vs. nice-to-have, with rough costs marked 'approx.').
2. Week-by-week plan for weeks 1-4: one focus per week and two concrete actions each.
3. Five common beginner mistakes and how to avoid them.
4. How to stay motivated when progress is slow: three tactics.
5. One simple metric to track.

Keep it practical and under 350 words; don't promise income or growth numbers.

new_title: Techniques to Remember What I Read
new_prompt:
I forget most of what I read in [kind of material, e.g. business books]. Give me memory techniques I can start tonight.

About me: [reading time per week, format: paper / e-reader / audio]

Output (under 200 words)
- 5 techniques as a numbered list. For each: name, how to do it in one sentence, and when to use it (during / right after / a week later).
- A 10-minute weekly review routine that combines them.
- One-line explanation of why spaced review works.

Prefer methods with good evidence (retrieval practice, spacing, summarising in your own words) over gimmicks.

new_title: Short Software Ad With Feature List
new_prompt:
Write a short advertisement for a software product.

Inputs
- Product: [name], a [what it is, e.g. sports team management app]
- Audience: [who]
- Main problem it solves: [problem]
- Key features: [3-5 features]
- Offer / CTA: [e.g. free 14-day trial]

Format (under 200 words)
- Headline (max 8 words) naming the benefit.
- Opening: 2 sentences on the problem, in the audience's words.
- Bulleted features, each turned into a benefit.
- One line of proof only if I give you real data (otherwise skip it; don't invent stats or testimonials).
- Clear call to action.

Give two headline alternatives at the end.

List the largest companies in a sector, with sources and dates.

Inputs
- Sector: [type of business]
- Country / region: [country]
- How many: [number]
- Ranking basis: [revenue / market cap / employees]

Output: a table with Rank | Company | One-line description | Founded | Current CEO | Ranking figure (with year).

Rules
- State the date your data is from, and flag anything that may be out of date.
- If you aren't sure of a figure or a CEO, write [VERIFY] instead of guessing.
- Suggest where I can confirm the figures (e.g. annual reports, stock-exchange filings).

new_title: Socratic Coach to Question My Thinking
new_prompt:
Act as a Socratic coach and help me test a belief.

Inputs
- Topic: [topic]
- My current view: [your view, 1-3 sentences]

Rules
- Don't tell me what you think and don't lecture.
- Ask one question at a time, then wait for my answer.
- Move through: why I believe it → evidence → assumptions → strongest counter-argument → what would change my mind.
- Point out contradictions gently; stay curious, not combative.

After about ten questions, give a summary: where my reasoning held up, where it was weak, the key assumption I rely on, and one source or experiment that could test it.

new_title: Blog Intro for a Game Design Idea
new_prompt:
Write the opening of a tabletop-gaming blog post that sells a game-design idea.

Inputs
- Idea: [e.g. countdown timers in encounters]
- Game system: [e.g. a fantasy tabletop RPG]
- Credit for the idea: [source, designer or game]

Requirements (max 150 words, one or two paragraphs)
- Open with a short scene played without the idea (flat), then the same scene with it (tense).
- Name the idea plainly and credit its source in one sentence.
- End with a line that makes the reader want the rest of the post.

Tone: enthusiastic, concrete, no jargon a new player wouldn't know.

Write a read-aloud poem for young children.

Inputs
- Topic: [e.g. what computers help us do]
- Age: [e.g. 4-6]
- One thing to teach: [e.g. computers follow instructions]

Requirements
- Four stanzas of four lines, AABB rhyme, a steady bouncy rhythm.
- Simple words a child of that age knows; no scary or sarcastic content.
- Include one repeated line or refrain the child can join in on.
- End with a gentle, positive message.

After the poem, suggest one simple action or question for the adult reading it.

Write a funny, loving letter to my pet.

Inputs
- Pet: [species, name]
- Their 'crimes': [3-4 habits, e.g. stealing socks, 5 am wake-ups]
- What I love about them: [2-3 things]

Structure (150-200 words)
1. Formal, mock-accusing opening, like a legal notice.
2. Itemised list of their crimes, with comic 'evidence'.
3. A turn: 'However…'
4. Heartfelt paragraph on why I love them.
5. A sign-off in the same playful-formal voice.

Keep it gentle; the teasing should feel affectionate.

Write the opening of a psychological suspense story in first person.

Inputs
- Narrator: [e.g. someone hiding a dark secret]
- Setting: [place and time]
- Length: [e.g. 300-400 words]

Requirements
- Build dread through what the narrator notices and how calmly they describe it, not through gore or explicit violence.
- Include one detail that seems ordinary but becomes disturbing on reflection.
- Keep the narrator's motives unclear.
- Stop at a cliffhanger; no resolution yet.

Avoid graphic harm, and give it a working title.

Rewrite an email so it sounds confident and direct while staying polite.

Inputs
- Email: [paste]
- What I need from the reader: [the decision or action]
- Relationship: [e.g. client, manager, vendor]

Rules
- Lead with the main point or request in the first two sentences.
- Turn hedges and questions ('I was wondering if…', 'maybe') into clear statements or requests.
- Keep every fact; add no new information or promises.
- Include a specific deadline if I gave one.

Output: the rewritten email, then a bullet list of the main changes so I can learn from them.

new_title: Three Quick Fixes for an Everyday Problem
new_prompt:
Help me solve a small everyday problem with three practical options.

Inputs
- Problem: [describe it in a sentence or two]
- Constraints: [budget, time, tools I have, living situation]

Output: three numbered options, cheapest or easiest first. For each:
- What to do (1-3 steps)
- Rough time and cost (mark costs 'approx.')
- One thing to watch out for
- How I'll know it worked

No preamble. If the problem could signal a safety issue (electrical, gas, health), say so first and recommend a professional.

Write the opening of a children's story about loss.

Inputs
- Character: [name, age, species]
- What they lose: [e.g. their old dog]
- Reader age: [e.g. 5-8]
